newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: State Dept seek immunity waiver for U.N. diplomats.
newsitem.headline: State Dept seek immunity waiver for U.N. diplomats.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Thursday it had asked Russia and Belarus to lift the immunity of two diplomats involved in a fracas with New York police last December.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said that after studying a police report on the incident, "we have formally asked Russia and Belarus to lift the diplomatic immunity of the two diplomats."
"They have not yet told us what they're going to do in these two cases," Burns told reporters in Washington.

Russia's U.N. ambassador Sergei Lavrov on Thursday firmly rejected charges from the New York prosecutor's office about the Russian involved, saying the man and his colleague from Belarus were beaten by police.
He said that a determination from the Manhattan District Attorney's office on Wednesday that the two should be prosecuted was "one-sided."

The Dec. 29 incident involved Boris Obnossov of Russia's U.N. mission and Yuri Orange of the Belarus mission, both first secretaries. Police said they pulled Obnossov from a car because he appeared intoxicated after parking illegally near a fire hydrant. Orange, who was travelling with Obnossov, was said to have punched one of the officers.

District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said the police acted reasonably and that the evidence would support criminal charges, including driving while intoxicated, resisting arrest, harassment and disorderly conduct.
According to Lavrov, Russia had received a fax from Morgenthau and "he clearly took one side and ruled that the diplomats were driving while drunk."

He said the incident happened after they left a restaurant and not while driving and that police prevented them from using the car afterward. Since the police never offered or gave the driver a test to determine if he was drinking "he cannot be accused of being drunk."
The district attorney, he said, "ignored all the evidence the Russian side provided and of a witness, an American witness, who saw what happened and contradicted the police report."
It was an "unjustifiable attack on Russian and Belarussian diplomats," he added.

Lavrov, this month's Security Council president, said Morgenthau had recognised in his statement the immunity provided for diplomats. "This immunity was taken from them when police decided to beat them on December 29," he said.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani followed up the incident by saying he wanted to remove the special license plates of diplomats who routinely ignore parking tickets, kicking off a dispute between the envoys and New York police and city officials.
Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, first agreed but then said the Giuliani plan should be modified. The issue still has not been settled.
Richardson said hostility toward foreign diplomats was increasing in New York, where police appeared to be harassing diplomats by deliberately targeting some of them in issuing parking fines.
The State Department has sought the lifting of diplomatic immunity in four alleged cases of drunk driving in the Washington area this year involving diplomats from the former Soviet Union.
But only in one case -- that of Georgian diplomat Gueorgui Makharadze, who was involved in a crash that killed a 16-year-old girl in January -- has the waiver been granted.
